title: The Real Cost of Food
hook: Why your grocery bill keeps climbing.

sections.title: Shrinkflation: The Sneakiest Price Hike
sections.content:
Have you noticed that your bag of chips feels lighter? That your cereal box has more air and less cereal? That your "half gallon" of ice cream is now 1.5 quarts? **You're not imagining things.** Welcome to shrinkflation — where companies keep the price the same but give you less product.

Shrinkflation is the corporate world's favorite inflation hack. Raising prices is visible and makes customers angry. Shrinking the product by 10% while keeping the same packaging? Most people never notice. A Snickers bar that weighed 58.7 grams in 2005 now weighs 52.7 grams. **That's a 10% reduction that no one voted for.** Gatorade bottles went from 32 oz to 28 oz. Doritos bags went from 10 oz to 9.25 oz. Charmin toilet paper has fewer sheets per roll. The list is endless.

But shrinkflation is just the visible tip of the iceberg. There's also **skimpflation** — where the product stays the same size but the quality drops. Cheaper ingredients, thinner packaging, less durable materials, worse customer service. That fast food burger tastes different than it did 10 years ago because the meat quality has quietly declined. Your "100% juice" has more water and filler than it used to.

Here's what's really happening: **the dollar is losing value, but companies can't just double their prices overnight.** So they find creative ways to give you less while appearing to charge the same. It's stealth inflation, and it's happening to virtually everything you buy. The official inflation rate says prices went up 3%, but when you factor in smaller sizes, lower quality, and added fees, the real cost increase is often double or triple the official number.

The government's Consumer Price Index (CPI) — the official inflation measurement — has been criticized for decades for **systematically underreporting inflation.** It uses tricks like "hedonic adjustments" (your TV is bigger, so even though it costs the same, they count it as a price decrease) and "substitution" (beef got expensive, so they assume you switched to chicken). The real inflation you feel at the grocery store is almost always higher than what the government reports.

sections.title: How Monetary Policy Affects Your Plate
sections.content:
Most people think food prices are driven by supply and demand — droughts, supply chain issues, bad harvests. And those factors matter. But the **biggest driver of rising food prices is monetary policy.** When central banks create trillions in new money, that money flows through the economy and eventually reaches commodity markets — including the markets for wheat, corn, soybeans, and every other ingredient in your pantry.

Here's the chain reaction: the Federal Reserve creates money and buys government bonds. Banks get more money to lend. Some of that lending flows to agricultural commodities traders. Prices for raw ingredients rise. Food manufacturers face higher input costs. They pass those costs to grocery stores. Grocery stores pass them to you. **By the time inflation reaches your shopping cart, it's been laundered through so many middlemen that the original cause — money printing — is completely invisible.**

The 2020-2022 period was a masterclass in this phenomenon. The Federal Reserve created over $4.6 trillion in new money. Within 18 months, food prices in the US jumped 10.9% — the highest annual increase in 40 years. Eggs nearly tripled in price. Butter, flour, and milk all saw double-digit increases. Politicians blamed supply chains, covid, and "corporate greed." But the elephant in the room was always the same: **you can't create trillions of dollars and expect prices to stay the same.**

Developing countries get hit even harder. When the US prints dollars, it doesn't just affect Americans. The dollar is the world's reserve currency — commodities like oil, wheat, and corn are priced in dollars globally. When the dollar supply expands, commodity prices rise worldwide. A family in El Salvador, Mexico, or Colombia feels the impact of American money printing at their dinner table. **The Federal Reserve's decisions affect what you eat for breakfast in Latin America, and you have zero say in the matter.**

This is fundamentally unfair and it's why food inflation is a moral issue, not just an economic one. The people who suffer most from food price inflation — low-income families, elderly people on fixed incomes, workers in developing countries — are the people with the least political power to change monetary policy. They didn't create the problem, but they pay the highest price.

sections.title: Food Costs Around the World
sections.content:
Food inflation isn't just an American problem — it's a global crisis that hits hardest in countries with the weakest currencies. Understanding how food costs vary around the world reveals a clear pattern: **the more a government prints money, the less food its citizens can afford.**

In **Venezuela**, years of extreme money printing made the bolívar so worthless that the cost of basic groceries became astronomical. A simple monthly grocery basket that once cost a few bolívares reached millions, then billions. Families were spending entire monthly salaries on basic staples like rice and beans. Some resorted to eating from garbage bins — not because food wasn't available, but because their money was worthless.

In **Argentina**, where annual inflation has regularly exceeded 100%, families have developed survival strategies that would seem absurd elsewhere. People rush to the grocery store on payday and buy everything they can, because by next week the same products will cost significantly more. Some stores change prices multiple times per day. Argentines have become expert inflation calculators — they can tell you exactly how many kilos of beef their salary buys, and they know that number keeps shrinking.

In **El Salvador**, where the average family spends over 30% of their income on food (compared to about 10% in the US), even moderate inflation is devastating. A 10% rise in food prices means families have to choose between eating less or cutting something else from their budget — school supplies, medicine, transportation. This is why El Salvador's adoption of Bitcoin as legal tender was so significant. It gave citizens an alternative to holding their savings in a currency being constantly eroded.

In **Mexico**, the price of tortillas — the most basic staple food — has become a political flashpoint. When tortilla prices rise sharply, protests follow. The government has repeatedly tried price controls, subsidies, and import programs, but nothing works long-term because the underlying cause — peso devaluation through monetary expansion — is never addressed.

The pattern is clear across every country: **when money loses value, food becomes unaffordable for the poorest citizens first.** Bitcoin can't grow crops or lower shipping costs. But it can protect the purchasing power of savings so that when you need to buy groceries next month, your money is still worth what it was worth this month. For billions of people around the world, that alone would be life-changing.
